title: Screencurve: an app that watches an episode and writes its format bible
excerpt: Screencurve analyses film and TV material and writes the format bible for an episode or a series. Every finding carries a timecode and a frame, so a producer can check it in the player.

signature.title: Every finding can be checked at its timecode
signature.body: An analysis nobody can verify is worth little on a real production. In Screencurve every statement about an episode carries a timecode and a frame. One click opens the scene in the player. The whole interface was designed around that rule.

challenge: What makes a format work is usually known only to the people who have watched it. That knowledge sits in notes and memory, and every new question about dramaturgy, characters or continuity starts another screening. A tool for this work has to earn the trust of production professionals: a claim about an episode counts only if it can be checked against the material.
solution: Screencurve takes an uploaded episode, reads image, sound, editing and dialogue, and writes a format bible. The chapters sit on two levels: the overview, the format bible and Ask the Film first, then three groups. Understand holds dramaturgy, characters, camera, editing, sound and production; Check holds compliance and continuity errors; Put to work holds the press release and the format and business view. Each finding carries its timecode and frame. Ask the Film answers questions about a cut in conversation and links every answer to the scene. A character constellation maps alliances and conflicts, the series analysis reads several episodes of a project together, and the archive makes every analysed episode searchable. Results export as Word or JSON. Production companies and groups have their own accounts, project access and credits. Only a proxy file reaches the model, storage and processing stay in the EU, and the material is never used for training.
